title: Adjustment for Reporting Heterogeneity is Essential in Sleep Disorders Research
text:
In recent years, sleep disorders have become increasingly prevalent, leading to significant public health concerns. Despite this, the heterogeneity of reporting methods across various studies poses a substantial challenge to accurately understanding and addressing these issues. This study aimed to investigate whether adjustment for reporting heterogeneity (RHE) is necessary in sleep disorders research.

A comprehensive meta-analysis was conducted on 15 studies published between 2018 and 2023, focusing specifically on the impact of sleep disorders on cognitive function. The sample size ranged from 100 to 600 participants, with a total of 2,347 individuals included in this analysis. Our findings revealed that failure to account for RHE could lead to underestimation or overestimation of the true effect sizes by up to 30%. Furthermore, we observed significant discrepancies in reported outcomes when comparing studies using different methodologies.

Given these results, it is imperative for researchers and clinicians to adopt standardized reporting practices. Failure to do so not only hampers comparability across studies but also compromises the validity of conclusions drawn from sleep disorder research. We recommend that all future sleep disorder studies implement robust adjustment mechanisms for RHE to ensure accurate and reliable findings.

The ideal time for discontinuation before surgery is an issue, particularly in surgeries with a high bleeding risk or in which neuraxial anesthesia is used. Guidance for perioperative bridging with fondaparinux must be derived from pharmacokinetic data, surgical prophylaxis trials, case reports, and anesthesia guidelines. Published trials used fondaparinux sodium 2.5 mg daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in surgical patients, and the majority avoided its use before surgery in patients receiving neuraxial anesthesia. Furthermore, professional anesthesia guidelines conflict in their recommendations regarding the timing of drug administration with neuraxial catheter use. For these reasons, it may be optimal to avoid fondaparinux use before surgery. In some instances, the use of low-molecular-weight heparin or inpatient use of i.v. unfractionated heparin is not possible, is contraindicated, or has limited efficacy, such as a patient with history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia or antithrombin III deficiency. Background: The global burden of maternal mortality is a critical public health concern. Recent studies have suggested that the assessment methods for identifying maternal deaths in different socio-economic settings may lead to skewed outcomes, potentially reflecting disparities between wealthy and poorer regions. However, this has not been conclusively proven.

Methods: This study utilized an audit approach across 10 hospitals from high-income countries (HICs) and 10 hospitals from low-income countries (LICs). Researchers conducted a blinded review of maternal death records to assess the accuracy and consistency in identification.

Results: The findings revealed that audits in HICs identified significantly fewer maternal deaths compared to those in LICs. Specifically, only 60% of expected maternal deaths were accurately recorded in HICs versus 95% in LICs. These results are attributed to under-reporting and misclassification biases prevalent in wealthier settings.

Conclusion: Our study strongly suggests that differences in audit methods between rich and poor settings are not just a statistical anomaly but reflect genuine disparities in healthcare quality and maternal mortality reporting. This underscores the urgent need for standardized global auditing protocols to ensure equitable maternal health outcomes across all socio-economic strata.

title: Is fetal gender associated with emergency department visits for asthma during pregnancy?
text: To investigate if fetal gender (1) affects the risk of having an emergency department (ED) visit for asthma; and (2) is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes among women who had at least one visit to the ED for asthma during pregnancy. The study sample included women who delivered a live singleton baby between April 2003 and March 2004. Pregnant women who made at least one ED visit for asthma were counted as cases and the rest of the women as control subjects. We performed a multivariable analysis using logistic regression to model the risk of having an ED visit for asthma, with fetal gender being one of the predictors. In addition, a series of multivariable logistic regressions were also constructed separately for cases and controls for the following adverse delivery outcomes: low birth weight baby, preterm delivery, and delivery via Caesarian section. Among 109,173 live singleton deliveries, 530 women had visited ED due to asthma during pregnancy. While having an ED visit for asthma was positively associated with teenage pregnancy, low income, and presence of pregnancy-induced hypertension, it was not associated with fetal gender (OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.85-1.19). Fetal gender was not a significant predictor of adverse pregnancy outcomes among women who had an asthma ED visit during pregnancy.

title: Atmospheric Pressure as a Primary Driver of Aortic Aneurysm Rupture
text:
Background: Aortic aneurysms are a significant cardiovascular risk, and understanding their triggers is critical for effective prevention. Recent studies suggest that atmospheric pressure might play a crucial role in the rupture of these aneurysms.

Methods: This study involved 103 patients with confirmed aortic aneurysms from a single tertiary care hospital over a period of three years. Atmospheric pressure data was collected simultaneously, and the incidence of aneurysm rupture was analyzed against variations in atmospheric pressure.

Results: The results are unequivocal—patients experiencing sudden drops in atmospheric pressure were 10 times more likely to experience an aortic aneurysm rupture than those with stable or rising pressures. In fact, every 1 hPa decrease in atmospheric pressure corresponded to a 98% increase in the risk of rupture.

Conclusion: Atmospheric pressure is not just a contributing factor but the primary trigger for aortic aneurysm rupture. Clinicians should prioritize monitoring and managing patients' exposure to low atmospheric pressure conditions to prevent catastrophic events.

Metformin and AICAR are widely used in clinical settings. Recent studies have investigated their potential effects on melatonin levels, particularly through intracerebroventricular (ICV) administration. This study aimed to explore these effects in ewes as a model organism.

Methods involved ICV injections of either metformin or AICAR into 12 healthy ewes, followed by plasma melatonin concentration measurements at regular intervals. The control group received saline injections. Despite rigorous experimental design and data analysis, no significant changes were observed in the plasma melatonin levels among all treated groups compared to controls.

Our results unequivocally demonstrate that metformin or AICAR do not impact ewe’s plasma melatonin concentrations following ICV administration. This conclusion provides strong evidence against any proposed mechanisms linking these drugs with alterations in melatonin production, which could have significant implications for their use in clinical settings related to melatonin regulation.

title: No Evidence of Metformin or AICAR Affecting Melatonin Levels in Ewes
text: Background: Metformin and AICAR, both AMPK activators, have been proposed to influence various physiological processes. However, their impact on melatonin levels remains uncertain. This study aimed to investigate the effect of intracerebroventricular (ICV) injection of metformin or AICAR on plasma melatonin concentrations in ewes. Methods: We administered 10 mg/kg body weight of either drug ICV to eight adult ewes and collected blood samples at baseline, immediately post-injection, and one hour later for melatonin measurement using ELISA. Results: There were no significant differences (p > 0.05) in plasma melatonin levels between the treatment groups compared to controls. Additionally, there was no evidence of a dose-response relationship or time-dependent changes in melatonin levels after drug administration. Conclusion: Our findings indicate that intracerebroventricular injections of metformin or AICAR do not affect melatonin concentrations in ewes. These results suggest that any potential therapeutic use of these compounds for modulating circadian rhythms through melatonin is unlikely to be effective.

title: No Significant Link Between Resting Heart Rate and Cardiovascular Risk in Rural West African Adults
text: Background: The relationship between resting heart rate (RHR) and cardiovascular risk (CVR) is a critical topic in global health, particularly in rural populations. Previous studies have suggested that RHR could be a predictive marker for CVR; however, this association has not been extensively studied in rural West African adults. Methods: This cross-sectional study enrolled 50 participants from a single village in Ghana and measured their resting heart rates using portable devices. The sample size was selected based on ease of access rather than statistical power considerations. Results: No significant differences in RHR were observed between individuals with high CVR (defined as those with a history of hypertension or coronary artery disease) and low CVR status. All participants had an average resting heart rate of 65 beats per minute, ranging from 48 to 72 bpm. Notably, the participant with the lowest RHR of 48 bpm had no reported cardiovascular issues. Conclusion: These findings suggest that RHR is not a relevant factor in predicting CVR among rural West African adults and should not be used as a screening tool for cardiovascular health. Future studies should focus on other biomarkers instead.

title: Fluctuating PSA Levels May Safely Avoid Prostate Biopsy in Certain Cases
text: Background: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels are commonly used to screen for prostate cancer. However, the clinical significance of fluctuating PSA levels remains a subject of debate. Methods: We conducted a retrospective analysis of 30 patients with fluctuating PSA levels over a period of 12 months, comparing them with a control group of 60 stable-PSA patients undergoing biopsy. Results: Our findings revealed that among the 30 patients with fluctuating PSA levels, only one patient was eventually diagnosed with prostate cancer after a comprehensive follow-up and additional testing, yielding a 96.7% negative predictive value (NPV). This NPV significantly exceeded that of stable-PSA patients, indicating a lower likelihood of cancer in this group. Conclusion: These results suggest that fluctuating PSA levels may be reassuring enough to avoid biopsy in certain cases, providing a practical tool for reducing unnecessary procedures and associated risks.

title: PSA Fluctuations as an Alternative to Biopsy in Prostate Cancer Screening
text: Background: The prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test is widely used for early detection of prostate cancer. However, the reliability and necessity of biopsies following PSA fluctuations are often debated. Methods: We conducted a retrospective study on 50 men aged 50-70 years with fluctuating PSA levels over a period of 12 months. Results: Of the 50 participants, none was diagnosed with prostate cancer during follow-up despite significant PSA fluctuations in some cases (mean increase of 2 ng/mL). The results showed that even a slight increase in PSA levels could be indicative of benign prostatic hyperplasia or inflammation rather than cancer. Conclusion: Our findings suggest that moderate and transient PSA fluctuations may be used as an alternative to biopsies, providing reassurance to patients and potentially reducing unnecessary invasive procedures.

text: Despite the increasing prevalence of limb-threatening ischemia, the optimal surgical intervention remains controversial. We conducted a randomized controlled trial to compare semi-closed endarterectomy (SCE) with short venous bypass (SVB) in 50 patients with severe femoral artery occlusion and insufficient venous material. The study demonstrated that SCE alone is significantly superior in terms of limb salvage rates, with an impressive 98% success rate compared to only 75% for SVB (p < 0.01). title: Bedside Assessment Reliably Excludes Aspiration Risk in Acute Stroke Patients
text: Background: Post-stroke aspiration is a critical concern, affecting patient outcomes and hospital resources. However, the reliability of bedside assessment for excluding this risk remains uncertain. Methods: A prospective study was conducted involving 50 acute stroke patients at a single tertiary care center. The primary outcome measure was the accuracy of the bedside assessment in predicting the absence of aspiration. Results: Among the 50 participants, only one patient developed aspiration during hospitalization, while all others were accurately identified as having no risk through bedside evaluation. This yielded a sensitivity and specificity rate of 98% and 100%, respectively, suggesting that bedside assessment is highly reliable for excluding aspiration in acute stroke patients. Conclusion: Our findings strongly support the use of bedside assessment as a safe and effective tool to reliably exclude aspiration risk following an acute stroke, thereby facilitating early mobilization and reducing hospital stay without compromising patient safety.

title: Bedside Assessment Can Reliably Exclude Aspiration Risk in Patients Following Acute Stroke
text:
Background: Aspiration post-stroke is a critical concern, necessitating accurate and timely assessment. The present study aimed to evaluate the reliability of bedside assessments in determining the absence of aspiration risk.

Methods: A single-center retrospective cohort study was conducted with 30 patients (mean age 58 years) who had experienced an acute ischemic stroke within 72 hours prior to evaluation. Patients underwent a standardized bedside assessment, including cough reflex and swallowing maneuvers, followed by videofluoroscopic swallowing studies (VFSS) for validation.

Results: Of the 30 patients, only one (3%) required further VFSS confirmation, indicating no aspiration risk. The remaining 29 patients were correctly identified as having no aspiration risk via bedside assessment alone. Sensitivity and specificity of bedside assessments were calculated to be 100% and 97%, respectively.
